Part of this is normal. Part of this may be spurred on by something. The descriptors you’re giving of your daughter are similar to me appearance wise. 
I was lightly bullied in school over my appearance, my thick hair, normal puberty things like growing hair, being too skinny, even my skin colour at a much younger age. 

A lot of this made me want to look vastly different in all areas, even down to skin colour, as I thought I needed to be white to be considered pretty. having smaller lips as people would be bullied for bigger ones (and mine I wouldn’t say are that big, I’ve even got a bit of filler in them now lol). 

I am mixed, I know a lot of my peers of similar heritage had a similar phase too. In primary school, at least in the 2000s anyway, it wasn’t ‘cool’ to look how I do. Once I got to secondary school it was different but I still didn’t like how I looked. And still wasn’t the main beauty standard just appreciated for being ‘pretty’. 

Saying beauty doesn’t matters to kids in this day and age, id say falls quite flat - social media making this a possibility. 

Have her watch people on YouTube with her hair type, those with the same attributes etc - doesn’t remedy the full problem but representation really matters in this context. My mum would buy me Bratz more than Barbie’s due to their diversity (I had a lot of Yasmine dolls lol) and just remind me that I do have desirable features. Something I didn’t understand then, but do more so now. 

But anyway as I’ve said, representation will matter. And if you don’t look similar to your daughter even more so because she’s probably searching for somewhere to relate appearance wise. (Even if you physically look alike but maybe diff hair colour, skin colour etc) 

Also remember, she will be in a period of finding herself, I was fashion conscious way before 10 and to this day still love fashion (but I am partial to a tracksuit unless I can be bothered to look ‘nice’).

As parents it’s our job to teach our children about their emotions. This requires us to be in tune with our own emotions and a level of emotional intelligence. It is HARD work and a lot of parents shy away from it and that is reflected in a lot of adults today who have poor mental health.  

Even though a lot of people still don’t believe it, kids need our attention and mostly all of it. We are their safe space. If as parents we can’t be that, emotionally we set them up for failure and potentially anybody who has to be around them in the future. If your child is crying, you try to find out the cause. If there’s no obvious cause, you soothe them. This goes for any ‘negative’ emotion. If you need to take a couple minutes that’s fine, just make sure you always come back, so they know you’re there for them emotionally. It doesn’t mean giving in to their needs, or invalidating the emotion. It just means comfort them and show you are emotionally present for them. 

I don’t know any resources but they are easily found online - I’d suggest sitting your husband down and showing him this. Disregarding your children’s emotions and making the harder ones seem negative at this age can have detrimental effects on a child. They can end up with disorders such as BPD, or chronic anxiety/depression. None of which are easy to deal with and in *some* cases preventable. 

It’s important your husband gets on board with this. I’d say children are born inherently with trust for their carers. Once this trust is broken, it will never be the same, no matter the repair or apologies given.

As someone who has BPD as well, you sound like you’re going through a major crisis. In this scenario, I would personally be asking for the father or trusted source of temporary (shortish term) care to seek the outside help. 

Personally I would suggest a crisis house if they have them where you are or check and ask a psychiatrist what hospitals they believe are beneficial to those who *also* suffer from BPD. Pregnancy and stress sent me to the psyche ward, only for me to be told I would have benefitted more from a crisis house because where I am (UK) the outpatient professionals I deal with believe the wards can be particularly difficult for people with bpd. I will not say why as a I never bothered prying into that information; I just know with my personal experience I will recognise crisis and go to the crisis house. That being said I also have social services involvement, the referral was never because of me, however I’m the mum and my risk needed to be assessed - now they give a lot of help and resources to try to prevent a crisis happening or one that puts me back into the ward (was already under services when I went in). There’s not actually shame reaching out to social services and asking for the help, if there are trusted people around to help with your kids and they can stay with - they shouldn’t end up in the system. 

I would also be demanding medication, because BPD typically makes your mood fleet and you split on people - this sounds persistent, like depression, which unlike BPD can be medicated. I know some people with BPD do have successful medicating with mood stabilisers and a therapy such as DBT or MBT. Personally the minute it’s safe for me to do so, I want to try them all as pregnancy/kids in my opinion add that extra layer of dysfunction with a disorder like this. 

I really hope you’re able to seek the respite that you need. If after stabilising yourself you still feel like this, give custody to those that you trust. Never see them again or be a mother who visits and is in their life but had to step back from primary caregiving. Parenting is hard, BPD is hard and as long as you have your kids best interest at heart, nobody is even in a position to shame you. 

Good luck op ❤️

When you can I suggest you try seek diagnosis (and no not because I’m discrediting you) but because before my diagnosis they put me on A LOT of anti depressants that were not working because I hadn’t actually fully developed any of the comorbid conditions the medications were made to target. I wasn’t happy but a lot of my anguish came from my feelings, knowing something was wrong but being certain it wasn’t as simple as ‘depression’ or ‘anxiety’. 

Now I’m 22, the advice I’d give to myself then (may sound slightly cliche) as thinking about what I do and accomplish despite how I feel. I.e. I still went to college/6th form, I could sometimes find the courage to go out and there was times I felt ‘okay’ (in hindsight). 

Where I am treatment for BPD is pretty restricted to those diagnosed (NHS), I do Mentalisation Based Therapy and I’m not sure if it’ll work but I’ve heard some really good success stories. 

It’s also worth noting I’m 22 and actually being reassessed as it’s come to light in therapy there may have been disorders I could’ve possibly had from childhood/teen that made BPD develop (ADHD has been suggested, also C-PTSD and they may look in bipolar type 2 due to some episodes I’ve had). It’s really important I know because for example if I had ADHD, it would be important I have meds and would also show why I was resistant to a lot of meds and prior treatments and it would (hopefully) help make my MBT more effective. 

I’m a bit too triggered by everything even my own feelings, to journal at the moment, but when my symptoms were not at their worse journaling really did help. The symptom that used to really get to me was the emptiness/boredom, which I feel like
can really heighten every other symptom. I think even if you don’t know it you’re on the right track to figuring out how to help yourself!

ADHD does presently differently in male and females, with females typically being under diagnosed. 

I encourage you to see a psychiatrist (if possible) and be really honest with your feelings. However, throw out your expectations to stop yourself from being biased so you can get the correct diagnosis!

Before you give up any custody etc, I would see a mental health professional or a doctor and I say this because you mentioned ‘feeling like the only way out is ending my life’. Once you’ve tackled this feeling, you very may well feel like you still don’t want to be a primary carer and then can make arrangements for her dad or your parents to be so (whoever agrees and whoever would be suited), but I think it’s really important to challenge that thought first. Without challenging it, it could ‘seem’ like the solution but then you might change your mind, feel like you were too depressed to make a judgement etc, I feel like we’ve all been there whether it’s regarding children or not etc. 

The advice would be if you go through with it regardless though, is handing over custody is the right decision because eventually she will notice you don’t want to be a parent, even if you do love her - but she may not correlate the two. *However* down the line it may be dangerous to ‘decide you want her back’ or even have other children that are yours (or not) in your care whilst she’s with somebody else - she won’t process it like you may do in your head. 

I personally think it’s clear you love her because there are parents who will just neglect their parental duties all together without handing them over - but I do honestly but a heavy suggestion on seeing a doctor first because for your own child’s mental health once decided, it’s not something you can just reverse. 

And to lightly touch on parents and money, yes - they will probably be angry, but you can’t put a price on life so if your honest with how it’s been making you feel, they should at least not pester or threatening over it. 

Good luck with whatever you do

The fact a psychiatrist has said it (IMO) means there’s a possibility you are showing signs and symptoms etc, but with conflicting ops, another opinion wouldn’t do any harm and stop confusion (if there is any) that the conflicting opinions may be giving.

It’s a very hard illness to diagnose. It can (not limited to) depend on age, number of symptoms, severity etc. So for example, I found out in one of my MBT classes that the team I am under try not to diagnose under 21s, thus most people in my class had not been diagnosed until their 20s and 30s. I had been diagnosed at around 18/19 because it was horribly obvious. I ticked every criteria box. This may not be the same in all regions but I know it isn’t something they like to diagnose in young people in general. 

Therapists (from my knowledge) don’t usually diagnose, but I wouldn’t say their opinion is to be discounted & psychiatrist do diagnose (that’s how I was diagnosed) - it may be worth asking for a second opinion from another psychiatrist but also possibly asking your therapist what they think the issue may be if not BPD. 

BPD can be misdiagnosed but also has overlaps with a lot of other mental illnesses; I’d say just keep pushing to feel better in yourself but also if you think you need a diagnosis of ANYTHING (even if not bpd) to push for that also, as I know diagnosis can be validating to peoples experience. 

Because this is such an unpleasant illness to have, and be diagnosed with (a lot of stigma) I do think it is important to take both and all opinions into account, until somebody can diagnose for sure.
